name: BFS / DFS on Graphs and Grids
description: Traverse a graph or grid to explore connectivity, shortest paths (unweighted), or connected components. BFS for shortest path/level-order, DFS for exhaustive exploration or backtracking-adjacent problems.
core_technique: BFS: queue-based, explore level by level, first time you reach a node is the shortest path (unweighted). DFS: recursive/stack-based, explore as deep as possible before backtracking, natural for marking visited regions.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to mark nodes visited before enqueueing (causes duplicate processing or infinite loops in cyclic graphs); using DFS when BFS is required for shortest-path correctness; not handling multi-source BFS when a problem has multiple starting points (e.g., rotting oranges).

example_problems.title: Number of Islands
example_problems.why_it_fits: Grid traversal, DFS/BFS from each unvisited land cell, mark connected land as visited -- classic connected-components-on-a-grid.

example_problems.title: Rotting Oranges
example_problems.why_it_fits: Multi-source BFS -- all initially rotten oranges start in the queue simultaneously, since they all rot neighbors at the same time step.

example_problems.title: Word Ladder
example_problems.why_it_fits: Shortest transformation sequence in an unweighted implicit graph -- BFS guarantees shortest path in terms of number of transformations.

additional_considerations: For grid problems, watch for whether diagonal moves count as adjacent. For multi-source BFS, seed the queue with ALL sources before starting the traversal, not one at a time -- this is the most commonly missed detail.
